content.thinking:
I need to fill in root_cause, executive_summary, and assumptions without restating the given figures as if I'd computed them myself, since the actual cost was derived from what the shop took in — so I should keep the narrative free of invented numbers and avoid presenting borrowed figures as my own calculation.

For the executive summary, I can state the factual time window (22:29–22:36) and describe elevated errors qualitatively rather than quantifying impact, referring to components generically as "the online shop's storefront" and "an internal pricing system." The root cause centers on the upstream pricing service degrading and adding latency to basket-total calls, resolved by a restart, with no code or config change found. Assumptions should note the causal link is inferred from correlation rather than proven, the underlying pricing-service fault wasn't identified, only a 155-minute lookback was checked for changes, and the pre-existing ClientDisconnected errors are assumed unrelated.

assumptions: io-pricing is assumed to be the faulty component. This rests on correlation: its slow responses coincided with the latency rise, and io-shop recovered after it was restarted. No direct evidence from inside io-pricing (its own metrics, logs, or resource state) was gathered, so the underlying fault there is unknown and could recur.
Change events were queried only for the 155 minutes before 22:34 and only for io-shop; an older change, or a change to io-pricing, would not have appeared in that window and has not been ruled out.

The ClientDisconnected errors on account pages appear in the logs both before and during the incident and are assumed to be pre-existing background noise (shoppers abandoning slow or normal page loads) rather than a symptom specific to this fault.
Recovery is taken from the service returning to its baseline metrics at 22:36; no check was made that in-flight or failed shopper requests during the window were retried or completed successfully.

The alternative explanation the investigator raised - that io-pricing was healthy and the slowness lay in io-shop's own call path to it - was not independently tested before the restart, so it is assumed to be excluded only by the fact that the restart worked.
input.executive_summary: Starting at 22:29 UTC on 28 September 2026, the shopping site became slow for customers, with basket and account pages taking noticeably longer to load and a modest share of requests failing outright. The cause was an internal pricing system the storefront depends on to calculate basket totals: it began responding very slowly, and within a minute every basket-total lookup was affected. The storefront's own software had not been changed or reconfigured, so nothing on its side triggered the problem. An automated responder picked up the alert at 22:34, identified the pricing dependency as the likely cause within about a minute, and restarted it. Normal performance returned by 22:36 UTC, roughly seven minutes after the problem began. A draft code change intended to make the storefront more resilient to a slow pricing service has been opened for review.
input.root_cause: io-shop's p50/p95/p99 latency rose sharply at 22:29 because calls to its internal upstream dependency, pricing.io-internal.svc (io-pricing), began taking roughly 1500ms on /v1/…/basket-total — affecting a minority of requests in the first minute and then effectively all of them from 22:30 onward. No deploy, release, or feature-flag change was found on io-shop in the hours before onset, so the degradation originated inside the pricing dependency itself; restarting io-pricing returned io-shop to baseline, though the fault within io-pricing that caused the slow responses was not itself identified.
